issues.description: The manuscript gives conflicting statements about the central aim: it first says the goal is to determine whether moral incongruence generalizes to other addictions, but later states a specific goal of demonstrating uniqueness to compulsive sexual behaviors. This risks confirmation bias and makes the registered hypotheses appear oriented toward proving a preferred outcome rather than testing competing explanations.
issues.quote: "The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence ... is uniquely related to sexual behavior, or if it generalizes to other addictions as well." ... "with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors."

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly defines moral incongruence as the interaction between behavioral frequency and moral disapproval, but later defines it as the interaction between moral disapproval and severity of consequences. These are substantively different constructs: consequences/problem severity is closer to the outcome and can create tautological or collider-type problems if used as a predictor. Even if the later phrase is a mistake, it creates ambiguity about the preregistered operationalization.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior)" ... "Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action."

issues.subcategory: interaction term may not measure incongruence
issues.description: Operationalizing moral incongruence as a product of moral disapproval and frequency assumes that higher values on both variables index mismatch, but an interaction coefficient in a regression is not itself a direct measure of value-behavior discrepancy. It tests moderation of a frequency-problem association by moral disapproval. This may not capture subjective incongruence, internal conflict, distress about mismatch, perceived violation of values, or attempts to abstain. Conclusions about 'moral incongruence' may therefore overreach beyond the measured variables.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)"

issues.description: Moral disapproval for all focal behaviors is measured with a single item. Single-item measures cannot estimate reliability, may fail to distinguish moral beliefs from perceived harmfulness, legality, religious prohibition, stigma, personal preference, or social desirability, and may not be equivalent across pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drug misuse, and illegal drug use. This weakens construct validity and comparability across domains.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions... 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'"

issues.description: The moral disapproval items differ conceptually across behaviors. Alcohol is framed as 'drinking alcohol' generally, whereas prescription drugs are framed as 'for non-medical reasons' and illicit drugs are inherently illegal. Disapproval of illegal drug use may reflect law-breaking rather than morality of use; prescription drug misuse is already framed as misuse. These differences undermine claims that the same construct is being compared across addictive domains.
issues.quote: "I believe that drinking alcohol is morally wrong." ... "I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong" ... "I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong."

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST not validated for proposed uses
issues.description: The study heavily modifies the ASSIST, changes response categories, changes alcohol screening content, averages items with different time frames and scoring ranges, and extends the instrument to gambling and pornography despite lack of validation. The resulting scores may not have known psychometric properties or clinical interpretability, limiting conclusions about 'problematic use' or 'addiction' across domains.
issues.quote: "To assess substance use behaviors, we will use a modified version of the Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test..." ... "Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography"

issues.subcategory: averaging ASSIST items with incompatible scales and time frames
issues.description: The proposed problematic-use score averages three past-3-month frequency items scored 0-5 with two lifetime/past-3-month items scored 0, 3, or 6. These items have different response metrics, time frames, distributions, and meanings. Averaging them gives disproportionate weight to the 0/3/6 items and produces a score that is not the validated ASSIST scoring algorithm.
issues.quote: "Participants will respond to three frequency based questions... on a scale of 0 ... to 5... Participants will also respond to two questions... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged"

issues.subcategory: inconsistent response coding for frequency scales
issues.description: The manuscript states the modified frequency scale is 0 to 5 in some places and 1 to 6 in others. This matters for centering, interaction computation, interpretation, inclusion criteria, and replication.
issues.quote: "on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)" ... "on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)"

issues.description: The methods describe the Brief Pornography Screen as scored 0 to 2 and summed, whereas the supplemental materials show response options coded 0, 2, and 4. This changes the possible score range and interpretation of effects, including equivalence tests and power assumptions.
issues.quote: "on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed." ... "Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)"

issues.description: The methods describe PGSI response options as 0 to 3 and averaged, but the supplemental materials code the options as 0, 2, 4, and 5. The standard PGSI is usually scored 0-3 and summed; using 0/2/4/5 and averaging changes scale properties and cutoffs. This inconsistency undermines reproducibility and validity.
issues.quote: "on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged." ... "Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)"

issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index is described as averaged rather than summed, and the supplemental materials use nonstandard scoring. If the authors intend to use validated PGSI severity thresholds or compare to prior literature, altering scoring without justification threatens validity and interpretability.
issues.quote: "problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index... Responses will be averaged."

issues.description: The BPS includes an item about continuing pornography use despite guilt, and the PGSI includes an item about feeling guilty about gambling. These outcomes partly include moral-emotional content, which may inflate associations with moral disapproval and create criterion contamination. This is especially problematic when comparing whether moral incongruence predicts self-reported addiction.
issues.quote: "5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it." ... "Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?"

issues.description: Pornography and gambling are assessed with domain-specific validated scales plus modified ASSIST items, whereas substances rely on modified ASSIST averages. Different measures differ in item content, time frame, scaling, and inclusion of moral/guilt content, making cross-domain comparisons of interaction magnitudes difficult to interpret as evidence of uniqueness.
issues.quote: "Alcohol | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items"

issues.subcategory: frequency measures are coarse ordinal variables treated as continuous
issues.description: Behavioral frequency is measured on a coarse ordinal scale with unequal intervals ranging from never, once/twice, monthly, weekly, daily, to more than once per day. Treating these as continuous in OLS and interaction terms assumes equal spacing and linearity, which is implausible and could distort interaction estimates.
issues.quote: "participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)"

issues.subcategory: cross-sectional design cannot establish temporal ordering
issues.description: The study uses cross-sectional survey data. It cannot determine whether moral disapproval leads to perceived addiction, whether perceived problems increase moral disapproval, or whether both are caused by other factors such as religiosity, stigma, distress, or actual severity. The limitation is acknowledged, but the manuscript still uses language implying prediction and influence.
issues.quote: "This sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables."

issues.description: The manuscript uses causal language such as 'influences,' 'affecting,' and 'contributor' despite an observational cross-sectional design. Regression moderation cannot establish causal influence, especially when predictors and outcomes are self-reported at the same time.
issues.quote: "we seek to establish whether moral incongruence... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction"

issues.description: The planned models include only age, gender, and religiousness as covariates. Many plausible confounds could affect both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction/problems: actual disorder severity, psychiatric distress, shame/guilt proneness, political ideology, education, race/ethnicity, marital status, legal context, social desirability, treatment history, abstinence goals, and frequency/quantity/intensity of use. Minimal adjustment limits interpretability of moral disapproval effects.
issues.quote: "In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates"

issues.subcategory: sampling design confounded with gambling oversample
issues.description: The total sample combines a nationally matched U.S. sample with a large sports-wagering oversample. Analyses appear to treat the combined sample as 'American adults' without specifying weighting, stratification, or sample-source adjustment. The oversample will alter prevalence, distributions, covariances, and interaction estimates, especially for gambling and related behaviors.
issues.quote: "representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500)"

issues.description: Although the manuscript describes the sample as matched to U.S. representative norms and includes an oversample, it does not state whether analyses will use survey weights, post-stratification weights, YouGov matching weights, or design-based variance estimation. Without this, representativeness and standard errors cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms."

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as nationally representative, but the combined analytic sample includes a sports-wagering oversample and only matches age and gender are explicitly mentioned. Representativeness across race, education, region, income, religion, internet access, and selection into YouGov panels is not established.
issues.quote: "nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population" ... "target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender"

issues.description: The representative sample is said to match only age and gender. Given the constructs under study are strongly related to religion, political ideology, education, race/ethnicity, and region, matching only age and gender may leave substantial sample bias.
issues.quote: "match nationally representative norms for age and gender"

issues.description: The authors rely on YouGov proprietary quality controls and state they do not anticipate removing inattentive or invalid responses. No attention checks, speed checks, duplicate prevention, straightlining criteria, bot detection details, or exclusion rules are specified. This limits evaluation and replication of data quality procedures.
issues.quote: "certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses"

issues.description: The manuscript lacks expected information on sampling frame, invitation procedures, response rate, compensation, eligibility screening, exclusions, quota fulfillment, weighting, consent procedures, and IRB approval. These details are needed to evaluate selection bias and replicate the study.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study"

issues.subcategory: unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors assume no unplanned missingness because data are collected through YouGov. Forced responses can reduce item nonresponse but do not eliminate missingness from panel data, breakoffs, skipped conditional items, refused demographic variables, or invalid responses. No missing-data handling plan is provided.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data."

issues.description: The manuscript says only participants endorsing past-year use complete further problematic-use items, but later says key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. These contradictory statements affect effective sample sizes, missingness, zero-inflation, and interpretation of outcomes among nonusers.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use." ... "key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior."

issues.subcategory: contradictory inclusion criteria for pornography follow-up items
issues.description: The pornography section states that only past-year users complete subsequent items, while the data screening section says problematic use and moral disapproval measures will be administered to all participants. It is unclear whether nonusers will be included in models, assigned zero problem scores, or excluded.
issues.quote: "only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months... will complete the remaining items described below." ... "we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample."

issues.description: The manuscript refers to eight proposed outcomes and eight moderation analyses, but Table 1 lists seven target domains, with pornography and gambling each having two outcome measures. Depending on whether modified ASSIST outcomes for pornography/gambling are analyzed in addition to BPS/PGSI, the number of models is 7, 8, or 9. This ambiguity affects multiplicity, power, and preregistration specificity.
issues.quote: "each of the eight proposed outcomes" ... "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses" ... "Target Substance/Behavior | Measure of Problematic Use"

issues.description: The analytic plan says the eight moderation analyses correspond to target behaviors with pornography and gambling assessed using validated measures, but Table 1 also includes modified NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography and gambling. The plan does not clearly identify primary versus secondary outcomes for these behaviors.
issues.quote: "with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively)." ... "Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items"

issues.description: The manuscript states an Anderson-Hauck equivalence test with SESOI δ=.27, then says the equivalence region is based on β=.11. These are inconsistent unless δ is on a different effect-size metric, but the manuscript does not explain the conversion. This makes the equivalence criterion unclear and potentially wrong.
issues.quote: "with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27." ... "we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate... (β=.11"

issues.description: The manuscript equates ΔR2, f2, Cohen's d, and standardized beta values without fully specifying formulas, model context, or whether the d values are appropriate for interaction terms in multiple regression. For example, δ=.27, β=.11, f2=.016, and d=.25 are treated interchangeably as the SESOI. Mis-specified conversions could invalidate equivalence bounds and power calculations.

The authors say focal predictors and moderators will be centered, but also say key variables will be entered in raw form and their product computed. Later equivalence decisions are based on standardized effects. For interactions, the scale of inputs strongly affects the coefficient; without specifying whether predictors are standardized before forming products and how standardized interaction coefficients will be obtained, estimates and equivalence tests are not reproducible.
issues.quote: "focal predictors... and moderators... will be centered and their interaction term calculated" ... "key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed"

issues.description: The study plans multiple moderation models, multiple outcomes, several substances, direct effects, interaction effects, equivalence tests, and exploratory alternative equivalence tests. No familywise or false-discovery correction is specified for primary hypothesis tests. Holm adjustment is mentioned only for bivariate correlations. This increases false-positive risk and complicates interpretation of uniqueness claims.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses" ... "Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics"

issues.subcategory: open-ended supplemental analyses for assumption violations
issues.description: The plan states that if regression assumptions are violated, supplemental analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' but does not specify which alternatives will be used, what thresholds define substantial violations, or which result will be confirmatory. This leaves considerable researcher degrees of freedom after seeing data.
issues.quote: "in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate"

issues.description: If hypothesized null-equivalence findings for gambling/substances fail, the authors plan exploratory analyses redefining the equivalence region based on the observed pornography effect. This is outcome-contingent and data-dependent, which can rescue a uniqueness interpretation after the primary criterion fails. It should be clearly labeled exploratory and not used to support confirmatory claims.
issues.quote: "In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence... we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome."

issues.subcategory: alternative model triggered by low power
issues.description: The authors propose changing the equivalence region for underpowered behaviors rather than addressing the low precision directly. This creates different inferential standards across substances and makes null/equivalence conclusions noncomparable.
issues.quote: "Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly... test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI"

issues.subcategory: power calculations ignore oversampling and weighting/design effects
issues.description: Power estimates appear to use nominal effective N values from the combined sample and assume simple random sampling. If weights or matching are used, design effects may reduce effective sample size. If no weights are used, estimates are not population representative. Either way, the power analysis is incomplete.
issues.quote: "Effective N" ... "All analyses conducted using G*power; assuming α = 0.05, regression models with 6 independent variables"

issues.subcategory: effective N calculations inconsistent with inclusion criteria
issues.description: Effective Ns are calculated as percentages of the total N=4,000, including the sports-wagering oversample, but prevalence estimates are taken from population surveys. For gambling, an oversample is incorporated ad hoc. For other behaviors, prevalence in a sports-betting oversample may differ from the general population. These Ns may be inaccurate.
issues.quote: "Given prevalence estimates..." ... "Alcohol | 70% | 2800" ... "Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325"

issues.description: The analysis codes gender as binary male vs not-male. This collapses women and nonbinary/other gender participants, obscures group differences, and may not match hypotheses or YouGov gender categories. It also creates an underdescribed handling of nonbinary participants.
issues.quote: "gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)"

issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are drawn from panel data, but age derivation, gender categories, coding of missing/other responses, and timing of panel data are not fully specified. Because these are covariates in all models, coding decisions affect estimates.
issues.quote: "Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey)."

issues.subcategory: religiousness composite may be psychometrically inappropriate
issues.description: Religiousness is created by averaging standardized items with different ordinal response formats. The manuscript does not specify whether standardization is within sample, whether ordinal variables are treated as interval, how nonreligious respondents are handled, or whether measurement invariance across denominations/gender is considered.
issues.quote: "Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items"

issues.description: Problematic use scales are bounded, ordinal/semicontinuous, likely zero-inflated and highly skewed, especially for low-prevalence substances. OLS may produce biased standard errors, nonnormal residuals, and uninterpretable linear effects. The plan to test assumptions after data collection without prespecified alternatives is insufficient.
issues.quote: "As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function"

issues.description: The authors acknowledge likely inadequate power for prescription drug misuse and illicit drug use but still include them in hypothesis tests about uniqueness/non-equivalence. Low Ns and sparse outcome variability make interaction estimates unstable, especially with six predictors and ordinal measures.
issues.quote: "in the case of illicit drug use... and prescription drug misuse... it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required"

issues.description: Equivalence testing requires sufficient precision to conclude effects are practically null. The manuscript anticipates low power for some substances but proposes looser alternative equivalence bounds, which cannot support equivalence to null effects. This weakens conclusions that moral incongruence does not apply to those substances.
issues.quote: "For these analyses, we would therefore not be able to evaluate equivalence with a null effect."

issues.description: Frequency alone may not capture exposure severity for alcohol, gambling, pornography, or drugs. Alcohol quantity, gambling expenditure/losses, duration of pornography sessions, nicotine dose, and drug potency are important predictors of problems and may interact with morality. Using only broad frequency risks residual confounding and weak measurement of behavior.
issues.quote: "we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed)."

issues.subcategory: alcohol use frequency mismatched to alcohol problems
issues.description: The study intentionally departs from the NIDA Quick Screen's heavy-drinking threshold and uses any alcohol consumption frequency. Moral disapproval of any alcohol drinking may be high among abstinent religious groups, but alcohol-related disorder symptoms are more related to quantity, binge episodes, and impairment. This mismatch may bias comparisons with pornography and gambling frequency.
issues.quote: "for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed)."

issues.description: The supplemental materials for men ask about more than 5 drinks but label the row 'More than four drinks.' This is internally inconsistent and may cause programming or interpretation errors.
issues.quote: "IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)"

issues.description: The methods say gambling frequency will use a single item but then say an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials show only 'Gambled or placed bets at all.' It is unclear whether multiple gambling activities are measured separately or only a global item is used.
issues.quote: "We will assess gambling frequency using a single item." ... "To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken."

issues.subcategory: sports betting oversample affects gambling construct
issues.description: A sports-wagering oversample may contain people whose gambling profile differs from lottery, casino, or online gamblers. Combining them and using a global gambling moral disapproval item may obscure heterogeneity in gambling forms and moral evaluations.
issues.quote: "additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically"

issues.description: The study examines self-reported feelings/problems and screening scales, not clinical diagnoses. Yet the rationale and implications concern diagnostic criteria for CSBD and other addictive disorders. Without clinical interviews or clinician-rated impairment, conclusions about false-positive diagnoses or diagnostic caveats are indirect.
issues.quote: "the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings"

issues.description: The authors acknowledge the sample is population-based but still frame implications for treatment and diagnostic validity. Effects in general-population self-reports may not generalize to treatment-seeking individuals or clinically diagnosed cases.
issues.quote: "should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD"

issues.subcategory: overstatement that CSBD caveat implies unique moral role
issues.description: The claim that the presence of a moral-distress caveat in CSBD criteria suggests a unique role of morality is not necessarily justified. Diagnostic manuals may include caveats for historical, political, cultural, or nosological reasons rather than because the mechanism is uniquely present in CSBD. This premise may overdetermine the study's theoretical framing.
issues.quote: "This distinction is only made for CSBD and not present for any other recognized diagnosis... which suggests that moral beliefs about sexuality might play a unique role"

issues.description: The manuscript refers to cannabis, illicit substances, prescription drug misuse, alcohol, and nicotine as recognized addictive disorders, but the measured categories are broad behaviors/substances rather than DSM/ICD substance use disorders. 'Illicit drugs' combines heterogeneous substances with different dependence profiles, legal meanings, and moral valence.
issues.quote: "recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse)"

issues.description: Combining all illegal/illicit drugs into one category collapses substances with very different prevalence, social meanings, moral disapproval, risk, dependence liability, and symptom profiles. A single frequency, morality, and problem score may be uninterpretable.
issues.quote: "Illegal/Illicit Drugs"

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between 'prescription drugs' and 'prescription drug misuse/non-medical reasons.' Moral disapproval and frequency refer to nonmedical use, but Table 1 labels the target as prescription drug use/misuse. Ambiguity may affect participant interpretation and analytic labeling.
issues.quote: "prescription drugs" ... "Prescription Drug Use/Misuse" ... "Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons"

issues.subcategory: no preregistration repository or Stage 1 protocol details
issues.description: Although labeled a Registered Report/pre-registered design, the manuscript does not provide a registration URL, time-stamping information, immutable analysis scripts, or clear distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses. These omissions reduce transparency.
issues.quote: "A Registered Report" ... "pre-registered design"

issues.description: For pornography and gambling, both validated scales and modified ASSIST outcomes are mentioned. The manuscript does not clearly designate which is primary for each confirmatory hypothesis or how discordant results will be interpreted. This allows selective emphasis.
issues.quote: "Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items"

issues.description: The manuscript says correlations will be reported using 'Holm-adjusted test statistics.' Holm adjusts p-values, not the correlation coefficients or test statistics themselves. This is likely imprecise reporting but should be corrected for clarity.
issues.quote: "Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics"

issues.description: The manuscript lists regression assumptions but does not define diagnostic methods or thresholds for linearity, homoscedasticity, independence, or normality, nor does it specify what constitutes 'substantially violated.' This undermines reproducibility.
issues.quote: "assumptions of regression... will be tested... in cases where assumptions are substantially violated"

issues.subcategory: independence assumption may be inappropriate for matched/weighted panel data
issues.description: The independence of residuals assumption may be affected by survey design, matching, quotas, clustering within panel strata, and repeated panel participation. The analytic plan treats observations as independent and does not account for design features.
issues.quote: "assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity, independence of residuals...) will be tested"

issues.subcategory: no attention to social desirability or stigma bias
issues.description: All measures involve stigmatized behaviors and moral judgments. Without measures or procedures addressing social desirability, anonymity assurances, or mode effects, responses may be biased, especially for pornography, illicit drugs, gambling, and moral disapproval.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling"

issues.subcategory: time-frame mismatch among predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Frequency and moral disapproval are assessed for the past year/current belief, BPS uses the past 6 months, ASSIST problem items use the past 3 months plus lifetime/past-3-month items, and PGSI uses the past 12 months. These nonparallel time frames may distort associations and cross-domain comparisons.
issues.quote: "past 12 months" ... "In the last 6 months" ... "In the past three months" ... "Has a friend or relative... ever"

issues.subcategory: possible reverse causation from problems to moral disapproval
issues.description: People experiencing harms from a behavior may come to view that behavior as morally wrong. The design does not separate preexisting moral disapproval from moral evaluations caused by negative outcomes, making it difficult to interpret moral disapproval as an antecedent moderator.
issues.quote: "moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems"

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval of own behavior vs behavior generally
issues.description: The items ask whether a behavior is morally wrong in general, not whether the participant morally disapproves of their own behavior or experiences personal incongruence. General moral judgments may not map onto personal distress or value-behavior conflict, particularly for substances used medically, culturally, or socially.
issues.quote: "I believe that pornography use is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: uniqueness inference requires direct comparison not only separate significance tests
issues.description: The hypotheses infer uniqueness if the pornography interaction is significant and other interactions are equivalent to zero. However, robust claims of uniqueness also require direct statistical comparisons of interaction effects across domains measured comparably, including uncertainty and measurement differences. The planned approach partly addresses this only through exploratory, data-dependent equivalence regions.
issues.quote: "should we find that moral incongruence... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence"

issues.description: The manuscript does not specify alpha for equivalence tests, whether one-sided tests are used, whether confidence intervals are 90% or 95% for TOST/Anderson-Hauck, or how p-values and CIs will be interpreted when significance and equivalence conflict. This limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: "Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect... fall fully within our equivalence region"

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding irrelevant/unaddressed but survey self-report risk remains
issues.description: There is no experimenter blinding issue in a self-administered survey, but the manuscript does not discuss whether analysts will be blinded during data cleaning or whether confirmatory analysis scripts will be finalized before accessing outcomes. In a registered report, this is important for reducing analytic bias.
issues.quote: "Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format... SPSS will be used to transform... data will be imported into and analyzed using R"

issues.description: The plan names SPSS, R, psych, stats, Interactive Shiny, and reg.equiv.fd but does not provide R version, package versions, SPSS version, or exact functions/settings for all models. This may affect reproducibility, especially for equivalence testing.
issues.quote: "SPSS will be used... analyzed using R statistical software... psych package... lm function... reg.equiv.fd function"

issues.description: Table 2 contains duplicated footnote text repeated across columns, making the table difficult to interpret and raising concern about manuscript preparation and reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: "1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey... | 1. All substance estimates based... | 1. All substance estimates based..."

issues.description: Several typographical errors reduce clarity, including missing words and incorrect terms. Some are minor, but in methods sections they can obscure intended analyses.
issues.quote: "the role moral incongruence in predicting" ... "Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence" ... "validate measures"

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency limited to solitary viewing
issues.description: Pornography frequency is measured as viewing pornography alone, despite the definition allowing partnered or general viewing. If participants use pornography with partners, their frequency and incongruence may be underestimated. This may affect comparisons and model estimates.
issues.quote: "Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)"

issues.subcategory: pornography definition may exclude audio/textual sexual media
issues.description: The definition focuses on films, clips, or pictures displaying the genital area and may exclude erotic text, audio, cam interactions, or non-genital sexually explicit content. This limits construct coverage and comparability with participants' own understanding of pornography.
issues.quote: "pornography refers to any sexually explicit films, video clips or pictures displaying the genital area"

issues.subcategory: conditional gender-specific alcohol questions exclude nonbinary respondents
issues.description: Heavy-drinking questions are triggered only if gender equals woman or man. Participants with other gender identities may not receive any heavy-drinking quantity item, and the manuscript does not explain how they are handled.
issues.quote: "IF GENDER = WOMAN" ... "IF GENDER = MAN"

issues.subcategory: modified frequency option unsuitable for episodic behaviors
issues.description: The 'more than once per day' category is useful for nicotine but less meaningful for alcohol, gambling, illicit drug use, and pornography, and it does not capture session length or amount. A common scale across domains may create superficial parallelism while sacrificing domain-specific validity.
issues.quote: "we will modify response options by adding an additional frequency category of more than once per day"

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only cultural context limits moral conclusions
issues.description: Moral disapproval and addictive-behavior stigma vary by country, religion, law, and culture. The manuscript acknowledges U.S.-only sampling, but some claims about ICD-11 and addiction broadly may overgeneralize beyond the sampled context.
issues.quote: "such a sample represents only one broad cultural context"

issues.description: The manuscript states self-reported pornography addiction likely reflects psychopathology regardless of whether it reflects dysregulated use. This conflates distress, moral conflict, perceived addiction, and clinical psychopathology; distress alone may not indicate a mental disorder, particularly in the context of moral disapproval.
issues.quote: "self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography likely reflects psychopathology, regardless of whether or not such self-reports universally reflect dysregulated use"

issues.description: The proposed observational self-report study cannot validate or invalidate ICD-11 diagnostic caveats. Finding domain-specific interactions would be only indirect evidence and would not establish that moral distress should or should not be included in diagnostic criteria.
issues.quote: "this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model" ... "additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11"

issues.subcategory: covariate adjustment may induce overcontrol for religiousness
issues.description: Religiousness is likely a major antecedent of moral disapproval. Adjusting for religiousness when estimating moral disapproval effects may remove meaningful variance in the construct of interest or create interpretational ambiguity, depending on whether the target estimand is total or direct effect of moral disapproval net of religiosity. The manuscript does not justify this estimand.
issues.quote: "we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates"

issues.description: Cannabis moral disapproval and use frequency are likely influenced by state legality, medical-use status, and local norms. The study has state of residence but does not plan to account for legality, which could confound moral disapproval with legal status and access.
issues.quote: "given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S. and the now-widespread, legal use of THC"

issues.subcategory: no plan for participants with zero use if included
issues.description: If all participants receive problem measures, many nonusers should have structural zeros on problematic-use outcomes. The analysis plan does not specify whether models are restricted to users, include nonusers with zero outcomes, or use hurdle/two-part models. Each choice addresses a different question.
issues.quote: "for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample"

issues.subcategory: restriction to users can bias interaction estimates
issues.description: If analyses include only past-year users, conditioning on use may induce selection bias and limits inference to users rather than the population. If the moral disapproval variable affects abstention, excluding abstainers can distort associations between disapproval, frequency, and problems.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use."

issues.subcategory: no plan for measurement invariance across domains/groups
issues.description: The study compares effect sizes across behavior domains and demographic groups, but does not test whether outcome scales function similarly across gender, religiosity, or user subgroups. This is especially important when moral/guilt items may have differential item functioning.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses... corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest"

issues.subcategory: supplemental materials inconsistent with methods on ASSIST inclusion
issues.description: The methods say pornography and gambling will be included as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST, and supplemental ASSIST items do include them. But Table 1 and analytic plan do not consistently state whether these modified ASSIST scores are confirmatory outcomes. This impairs replicability.
issues.quote: "We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST"

issues.subcategory: power based on detecting effects, not equivalence precision
issues.description: The power analysis emphasizes power to detect f2=.015 in regression. Equivalence testing has different power requirements based on confidence interval width and equivalence bounds. The manuscript does not present power for the equivalence tests themselves for each behavior.
issues.quote: "we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest"

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of transformations and standardization
issues.description: The plan says SPSS will transform ASSIST items and religiousness into standardized variables, but it is unclear whether outcomes, predictors, moderators, or covariates are standardized, whether standardization is within full sample or analytic subset, and whether interactions use standardized or centered raw variables. This affects coefficients and equivalence tests.
issues.quote: "SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables."

issues.description: Moral disapproval, religiosity, and their interaction with frequency may be highly correlated, especially among pornography users. Centering helps but does not eliminate collinearity. The plan does not mention checking VIFs or stability of interaction estimates.
issues.quote: "religiousness, age, and gender as covariates... moral disapproval... frequency... interaction"

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval direct effects hypothesized across domains despite uniqueness claim
issues.description: The manuscript hypothesizes that direct moral disapproval effects will be positive for pornography, gambling, and substances, while interactions are unique to pornography. However, it sometimes frames moral incongruence and moral disapproval interchangeably. This may confuse theoretical interpretation: direct disapproval associations across domains would already suggest morality affects self-reported problems broadly.
issues.quote: "we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems"

issues.subcategory: problem outcomes include external concern item affected by stigma
issues.description: The ASSIST-derived outcome includes whether others expressed concern. This may reflect social norms and stigma around a behavior as much as impairment or addiction severity. Moralized behaviors may elicit more concern from others, inflating associations with moral disapproval.
issues.quote: "Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?"

issues.subcategory: legal/financial problems not applicable across domains
issues.description: The modified ASSIST consequences item asks about health, social, legal, or financial problems for all domains, including pornography and nicotine. Different domains have different likelihoods of legal or financial consequences, reducing comparability of scores across behaviors.
issues.quote: "health, social, legal, or financial problems"

issues.subcategory: no exclusion criteria for inconsistent responses
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify how it will handle inconsistent responses, such as reporting no past-year use but reporting urges/problems, or endorsing failed control for a behavior reportedly never used. Such inconsistencies are likely in survey data and affect scale construction.
issues.quote: "we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset"

issues.subcategory: larger parent study may introduce context/order effects
issues.description: The study is embedded in a larger sports-wagering survey. The order of measures, preceding questions, and survey framing may prime gambling/addiction concepts and influence moral disapproval or self-reported problems. The manuscript does not report measure order or context.
issues.quote: "as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors"

issues.description: Order effects are plausible when asking about moral disapproval, frequency, urges, and consequences for stigmatized behaviors. The manuscript does not specify the order of survey blocks/items or whether order is randomized.
issues.quote: "a number of measures enabling us to test the above hypotheses will be included"

issues.subcategory: ordinal reliability estimates with alpha/omega unspecified
issues.description: The plan computes Cronbach's alpha and omega total for ordinal scales with few response categories but does not specify use of polychoric correlations or ordinal omega. Standard alpha/omega using Pearson correlations can underestimate or misrepresent reliability for ordinal items.
issues.quote: "Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total"

issues.subcategory: BPS and PGSI timeframes do not match frequency moderators
issues.description: Frequency moderators are past-year, BPS is past-6-month, and PGSI is past-year. For pornography, the mismatch means someone with earlier-year use but no recent use may have frequency but no BPS symptoms; for gambling, the timeframe matches. This nonparallelism can affect cross-domain comparisons.
issues.quote: "past-year frequency of pornography use" ... "In the last 6 months"

issues.subcategory: planned sample size dictated by budget not inferential needs
issues.description: The target sample size is determined by budget/parent grant rather than the requirements of all confirmatory tests, and the authors acknowledge some key subgroups may be underpowered. This is problematic for strong claims about substances with low prevalence.
issues.quote: "Due to the budgetary constraints... the target sample size will be 2,500"

issues.description: YouGov panels are nonprobability internet panels using matching. The manuscript does not acknowledge selection bias associated with panel membership, internet access, willingness to disclose stigmatized behaviors, or survey-taking behavior.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling"

issues.subcategory: non-independence of multiple outcomes not modeled
issues.description: The same respondents provide data across multiple behaviors/substances. Separate regressions ignore within-person correlations and do not model person-level propensity toward moralization, distress, or response style. This can affect cross-domain inferences and multiplicity.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses"

issues.description: All key predictors, moderators, and outcomes are self-reported in the same survey. Shared negative affectivity, stigma, response style, and self-presentation may inflate associations between moral disapproval and self-perceived addiction.
issues.quote: "self-reported feelings of addiction" ... "single-item moral disapproval questions"

issues.subcategory: self-perceived addiction vs disorder symptoms conflated
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between self-reported feelings of addiction, problematic use, dysregulation, and disorder symptoms. The selected scales are screens or symptom/problem indices, not direct measures of self-perceived addiction for all domains. This weakens conceptual precision.
issues.quote: "self-reported feelings of addiction" ... "self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms" ... "self-reported symptoms of substance use disorders"
